name: Lata
definition: Lata is a composite portrait of a Kuruba woman in her mid-thirties working as a school cook and anganwadi helper in Saundatti taluk, Belagavi district, in the Kittur Karnataka region. She represents households navigating precarious daily-wage work, drought pressures, children's schooling hopes, and the social currents around the Yellamma temple town.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Lata rises before dawn to light the anganwadi stove and prepare the midday meal for the government primary school in her village, eight kilometres from Saundatti town. She earns around Rs 4,500 a month as an anganwadi helper and another Rs 3,000 cooking at the school under the akshara dasoha scheme, though payment often arrives two or three months late. Her husband Basappa works as a daily-wage labourer on neighbouring farms during the jowar and groundnut seasons and migrates to Goa construction sites from November to March, sending home Rs 6,000 to Rs 8,000 each month when work is steady. Lata supplements the household income by tending their one-acre rainfed plot, where they grow jowar and tur, and by collecting firewood from the scrub near Kappatagudda. The 2023 drought damaged their crop and they borrowed Rs 25,000 from a local moneylender at two percent monthly interest; the 2026 monsoon was again poor and the family now owes Rs 38,000. Lata walks to work, cooks on wood and LPG when the cylinder subsidy arrives, and spends evenings washing vessels, fetching water from the shared borewell, and minding the children.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Lata lives with her husband Basappa, their three children—a daughter Renuka aged fifteen, a son Manjunath aged twelve, and a younger daughter Kavitha aged eight—and Basappa's widowed mother, who is seventy and receives a Rs 1,000 widow pension that is often delayed. Renuka completed SSLC in 2026 with a second-class pass and now attends a government PU college in Saundatti town, travelling by NWKRTC bus using her new free student pass, though the family worries about hostel fees if she stays on for second PUC. Manjunath is in Class 7 at the village school where Lata works, and Kavitha in Class 3. Lata's mother-in-law helps with cooking and childcare but has chronic joint pain and needs the PHC at Saundatti every month. Household decisions about money, migration and the children's future rest largely with Basappa, but Lata manages the ration card, Gruha Lakshmi instalments, and dealings with the school and anganwadi.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Lata studied in Kannada medium at the village school up to Class 7, leaving when her parents needed her labour at home and saw no point in a girl continuing. She wishes she had reached SSLC. All three children attend the village government school in Kannada medium; the school has four teachers for eight classes, so Classes 6 and 7 share one room. Renuka passed SSLC in 2026 with 62 percent under the new 33-percent aggregate rule and joined first-year PUC science stream at Saundatti, hoping to reach nursing college. The Rs 1,500 bus fare each month was a burden until the student pass began, and Lata worries about textbook and tuition costs. Kavitha is bright but sometimes absent when the anganwadi closes or Lata is ill. Lata has heard of the Morarji Desai residential school and KGBVs but does not know the admission process. She receives Gruha Lakshmi—Rs 2,000 monthly when it arrives—and uses part of it for the children's notebooks, uniforms and shoes.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Lata and her family depend on the primary health centre at Saundatti, fourteen kilometres return by bus. Her mother-in-law's arthritis requires monthly painkillers and occasional referral to Belagavi district hospital, costing the family Rs 1,500 to Rs 2,000 each trip for transport, tests and medicines not available free. Lata herself suffers from anaemia—she was told her haemoglobin was eight during Kavitha's pregnancy—and chronic back pain from years of heavy work, but she rarely seeks care. Renuka began menstruating at thirteen and Lata bought her sanitary napkins from the ration shop when available, otherwise cloth. The village borewell water has a salty taste and some neighbours complain of joint pain, though no one has tested for fluoride. Dengue and diarrhoea cases rise in the monsoon; Kavitha had fever and loose motions in September 2026 and Lata took her to a private clinic in Saundatti, spending Rs 800. Basappa drinks occasionally and has had minor injuries on construction sites in Goa but no major illness. The family is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat but Lata has never used the card. She worries about the cost of any serious illness and the debt it would bring.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Lata's family belongs to the Kuruba community, listed as OBC Category 1 in Karnataka. Kurubas in the village work as labourers and small farmers; some families own two or three acres, most less. The village has a mix of Kuruba, Lingayat and SC Madiga households, and a small Maratha presence. Lata speaks Kannada at home and knows a few Marathi phrases from her mother-in-law, who grew up near the Maharashtra border. The family worships at the village Hanuman temple and once a year makes the pilgrimage to the Yellamma temple at Saundatti during the Bharat Hunnime fair in November, though Lata knows the devadasi history and is glad the practice is now unlawful. Her mother-in-law believes in the Mailara jatra and herbal remedies from the local vaidya. Lata participates in a women's self-help group organized by a local NGO; the group saves Rs 100 per member monthly and has taken a Rs 50,000 bank loan for joint ventures, though Lata's share was used to repay the moneylender. She has little contact with the gram panchayat beyond ration-card updates. Caste tensions are muted in daily life but Lata has heard of Panchamasali agitations in Belagavi and Kuruba families' demand for ST status, which she supports because it might help Manjunath get a quota seat.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Lata's household receives five kilograms of rice per person under Anna Bhagya, though the ration shop sometimes runs short and opens irregularly. She enrolled for Gruha Lakshmi in June 2023 and receives Rs 2,000 monthly, but payments have been delayed by two months twice in the past year; she uses the money for children's school costs and loan repayment. Renuka now travels free on NWKRTC buses under the student pass announced in June 2026, a relief Lata praises aloud. The family has a BPL ration card and Ayushman Bharat coverage but no land title—Basappa's father held the acre on a decades-old arrangement with a Lingayat landlord and the family has no patta. She has heard of the Kittur Rani Chennamma schemes but does not know what they fund. The anganwadi supervisor visits monthly and Lata must maintain records and cleanliness, but supplies of rice, dal and oil are often delayed. She wishes the gram panchayat would fix the village road and the hand-pump near her house. Basappa has worked ten days under MGNREGA this year at Rs 309 per day, paid after six weeks. Lata does not follow state politics closely but knows there is a new chief minister, Shivakumar, since June 2026, and hopes the government will not stop the guarantees.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Lata is proud that Renuka passed SSLC and reached PU college, something neither parent managed, and she is determined that Kavitha will study at least that far. She worries constantly about money—the unpaid anganwadi salary, the moneylender's interest, the cost of Renuka's textbooks and the question of where Manjunath will study after Class 10. Lata blames middlemen and the government for the low price of jowar and groundnut, and she resents that Gruha Lakshmi payments are delayed while the scheme is advertised on TV. Lata feels the government listens more to Belagavi city and Hubballi than to Saundatti taluk villages, and she has heard people say that Kalyana Karnataka gets special money under some central rule while Kittur Karnataka is ignored. She does not understand the politics but agrees something is unfair. She wishes her daughter could study without fear, her son could reach degree, and the family could clear its debt. What she wants from the government is regular payment of wages and Gruha Lakshmi, a proper bus service to Saundatti, a high school closer to the village, and a doctor at the PHC who is present when needed.
